# Creating summary files from large data sets

## Preliminaries

Let's start by making the Tidyverse available.

```{r}

# in case the Tidyverse is not installed on your computer, use the command below (just delete the hashtag)

install.packages("tidyverse")

# make the tidyverse available with the library function:
library(tidyverse)  
```

## Read in Drinking Water Data

Read in the data. If data includes zip code information, we need to make zip_code column "character" or zip codes starting with 0 are not read correctly

```{r}

#pb90_data <- read.csv("pb90_data_cleaned.csv", colClasses = c(zip_code = "character"))

lead_historical <- read.csv("lead_samples_historical_cleaned.csv")
```

```{r}

#this defines that data type in each column
str(lead_historical)

```

Look at data - sort by ppb

```{r}

# Sort by 'ppb' in descending order
sorted_lead_historical <- lead_historical |>
  arrange(desc(ppb))

# View the result
sorted_lead_historical
```

## Create Data Summaries to Use for Merging or Analysis

What years does the data cover? Create summaries based on "end_year" and "start_year"

end_year

```{r}

end_year_summary <- lead_historical |>
  group_by(end_year) |>
  summarize(avg_lead_ppb=mean(ppb), sd_lead_ppb=sd(ppb), median_lead_ppb=median(ppb))

end_year_summary
```

are there any trends? do a quick plot to find out

look at averages

```{r}

end_year_plot_avg <- ggplot(end_year_summary, mapping=aes(x=end_year, y=avg_lead_ppb))+
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = avg_lead_ppb - sd_lead_ppb, ymax = avg_lead_ppb + sd_lead_ppb))+
  geom_point()

end_year_plot_avg

#ggsave("end_year_plot_avg.jpg", end_year_plot_avg)
```

look at medians

```{r}

end_year_plot_med <- ggplot(end_year_summary, mapping=aes(x=end_year, y=median_lead_ppb))+
  geom_point()

end_year_plot_med

ggsave("end_year_plot_med.jpg", end_year_plot_med)
```

start_year

```{r}

start_year_summary <- lead_historical |>
  group_by(start_year) |>
  summarize(avg_lead_ppb=mean(ppb), sd_lead_ppb=sd(ppb), median_lead_ppb=median(ppb))

start_year_summary
```

are there any trends? do a quick plot to find out

look at averages

```{r}

start_year_plot_avg <- ggplot(start_year_summary, mapping=aes(x=start_year, y=avg_lead_ppb))+
#  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = avg_lead_ppb - sd_lead_ppb, ymax = avg_lead_ppb + sd_lead_ppb))+
  geom_point()

start_year_plot_avg

ggsave("start_year_plot_avg.jpg", start_year_plot_avg)
```

look at medians

```{r}

start_year_plot_med <- ggplot(start_year_summary, mapping=aes(x=start_year, y=median_lead_ppb))+
  geom_point()

start_year_plot_med

ggsave("start_year_plot_med.jpg", start_year_plot_med)
```

State Summary

```{r}

state_summary <- lead_historical |>
  group_by(state_abb) |>
  summarize(avg_lead_ppb=mean(ppb), sd_lead_ppb=sd(ppb), median_lead_ppb=median(ppb))

state_summary

write_csv(state_summary, "state_summary_historical.csv")

```

source of state_abb = NA

```{r}

na_states <- lead_historical |>
  filter(is.na(state_abb))
```

quick look at data - averages

```{r}

state_avg_lead_plot <- ggplot(state_summary, mapping=aes(x=avg_lead_ppb, y=reorder(state_code, avg_lead_ppb)))+
#  geom_errorbarh(aes(xmin = avg_lead_ppb - sd_lead_ppb, xmax = avg_lead_ppb + sd_lead_ppb))+
#  xlim(-10,20)+
  geom_point()

state_avg_lead_plot

ggsave("state_avg_lead_plot.jpg", state_avg_lead_plot)
```

quick look at data - medians

```{r}

state_med_lead_plot <- ggplot(state_summary, mapping=aes(x=median_lead_ppb, y=reorder(state_code, median_lead_ppb)))+
#  xlim(-10,20)+
  geom_point()

state_med_lead_plot

ggsave("state_med_lead_plot.jpg", state_med_lead_plot)
```

There's not that much variation by state (with the exception of a couple of outliers)

Try group by/summarize for each zip code

```{r}

zip_summary <- pb90_data |>
  group_by(zip_code) |>
  summarize(avg_lead_ppb=mean(sample_measure_ppb), sd_lead_ppb=sd(sample_measure_ppb), median_lead_ppb=median(sample_measure_ppb), data_points = n())

zip_summary
```

How many of the 21,518 zipcodes only have 1 data point (i.e., a standard deviation of NA)

```{r}

one_zip_code <- zip_summary |>
  filter(data_points == 1)

```

There are 1246 data points where there is just one zip code. Should I eliminate these points?

Create a new data set in which zip codes with only one data point are removed

```{r}

zip_summary_no_na <- zip_summary|>

  #drop_na() to remove row if any column contains NA
  
drop_na(sd_lead_ppb) #to remove row if column contains NA

#this removed 1246 data points

```

Save zip_summary and zip_summary_no_na as a csv files

```{r}

write_csv(zip_summary, "zip_summary.csv")


write_csv(zip_summary_no_na, "zip_summary_no_na.csv")
```

some of the lead concentration averages and medians are quite large; sort data by average and median to see what's going on

```{r}

# Sort by 'avg_lead_ppb' in descending order
sorted_zip_summary_avg <- zip_summary |>
  arrange(desc(avg_lead_ppb))

# View the result
print(n=100, sorted_zip_summary_avg)
```

A lot of the zip codes with the highest lead levels are from zip codes with only 1 data point

What happens if I do the same after removing zip codes where there is only 1 data point

```{r}

# Sort by 'avg_lead_ppb' in descending order
sorted_zip_summary_no_na_avg <- zip_summary_no_na |>
  arrange(desc(avg_lead_ppb))

# View the result
print(n=100, sorted_zip_summary_no_na_avg)
```

```{r}

# Sort by 'median_lead_ppb' in descending order
sorted_zip_summary_median <- zip_summary |>
  arrange(desc(median_lead_ppb))

# View the result
print(n = 100, sorted_zip_summary_median)
```

repeat for zip_summary_no_na

```{r}

# Sort by 'median_lead_ppb' in descending order
sorted_zip_summary_no_na_median <- zip_summary_no_na |>
  arrange(desc(median_lead_ppb))

# View the result
print(n=100, sorted_zip_summary_no_na_median)


```

It might also be interesting to just focus on a given state and then merge with census data by county or zip code. Below is an example where I select California

first filter pb90_data for state_code = CA

```{r}

pb90_data_ca <- pb90_data |>
  filter(state_code=="CA")
```

group by county

```{r}
county_summary <- lead_historical |>
  group_by(county_served, state_abb) |>
  summarize(avg_lead_ppb=mean(ppb), sd_lead_ppb=sd(ppb), median_lead_ppb=median(ppb), data_points = n())

county_summary
```

save county_summary

```{r}

write_csv(county_summary, "county_summary_historical.csv")

```

look at data - average sample measure

```{r}

ca_county_avg_lead_plot <- ggplot(ca_county_summary, mapping=aes(x=avg_lead_ppb, y=reorder(countyserved, avg_lead_ppb)))+
#  geom_errorbarh(aes(xmin = avg_lead_ppb - sd_lead_ppb, xmax = avg_lead_ppb + sd_lead_ppb))+
  xlim(0, 35)+
  geom_point()

ca_county_avg_lead_plot

#ggsave("ca_county_avg_lead_plot", ca_county_avg_lead_plot)
```

look at data - median sample measure

```{r}

ca_county_med_lead_plot <- ggplot(ca_county_summary, mapping=aes(x=median_lead_ppb, y=reorder(countyserved, median_lead_ppb)))+
#  xlim(0, 35)+
  geom_point()

ca_county_med_lead_plot

#ggsave("ca_county_avg_lead_plot", ca_county_avg_lead_plot)
```

now group CA data by zip code - all the zip codes have more than 1 data point so there is no need to remove NA points

```{r}

ca_zip_summary <- pb90_data_ca |>
  group_by(zip_code) |>
  summarize(avg_lead_ppb=mean(sample_measure_ppb), sd_lead_ppb=sd(sample_measure_ppb), median_lead_ppb=median(sample_measure_ppb), data_points = n())

ca_zip_summary
```

too many data points to look at a graph
